prompt: Some people think governments should invest more in public transport than in building new roads. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
body: It is often argued that building more roads is the quickest way to reduce congestion. In my view, however, public transport deserves the larger share of investment, because it addresses the cause of the problem rather than its symptoms, although some road spending remains necessary.

The main weakness of road building is that it tends to defeat itself. New roads tend to fill up within a few years, as cheaper and faster journeys encourage more people to drive. This effect, known as induced demand, has been observed in cities from Los Angeles to London, where widened motorways were soon as crowded as before. A well-funded metro network, by contrast, moves far more passengers in the same space, which would alleviate traffic for everyone, including those who still choose to drive.

Public transport also brings benefits that roads cannot match. A single train line can carry tens of thousands of commuters an hour while producing a fraction of the emissions of private cars. It also widens access to jobs and education for people who cannot afford a car, such as students and older residents. Singapore is a clear example: its decision to restrict car ownership and expand the MRT has kept the city moving despite its density.

That said, roads cannot be ignored entirely. Buses, delivery vehicles and emergency services all depend on them, and rural areas may never have enough passengers to justify rail. Spending on maintenance and on a few strategic links is therefore still justified.

In conclusion, while roads have a role to play, I strongly believe that the bulk of transport funding should go to public systems, since they offer a lasting solution to congestion and serve a far wider section of society.

prompt: Some people believe that university education should be free for everyone, while others think students should pay for their own studies. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
body: Whether university should be funded by the state or by students themselves is a question that divides many societies. Although there are reasonable arguments for asking students to contribute, I believe that tuition should be free, or close to it, for anyone with the ability to benefit.

Those who favour fees make two main points. First, graduates usually earn considerably more over their lifetimes than non-graduates, so it seems fair that they, rather than taxpayers who may never have attended university, should bear the cost. Second, paying for a course can make students more committed: someone who has taken out a loan is arguably less likely to drift through their degree or choose a subject without considering its value.

On the other hand, supporters of free education argue that the benefits of a degree do not stay with the individual. Society as a whole gains from trained doctors, engineers and teachers, and from the higher taxes that graduates pay. Moreover, fees can discourage talented young people from poorer families, who are often more reluctant to take on debt than their wealthier peers. If university becomes a privilege of those who can pay, a country wastes much of its potential.

In my opinion, the second argument is more convincing. The fairness concern can be met through a progressive tax system, under which high-earning graduates already contribute more. Free tuition, combined with entry based on merit, keeps opportunity open without placing the burden on eighteen-year-olds.
In conclusion, while I understand why some people feel students should pay, I believe that the wider social benefits of higher education justify public funding.

prompt: More and more people are working from home rather than in an office. Do the advantages of this trend outweigh the disadvantages?
body: Since the pandemic, working from home has moved from a rare perk to a normal arrangement for millions of office workers. While this shift has real drawbacks, I would argue that its advantages are greater, provided that companies manage it sensibly.

The most obvious benefit is time. Employees who no longer commute can save an hour or more each day, which they can spend resting, exercising or with their families. This tends to improve both well-being and productivity, as people start work less tired and less stressed. Remote work also widens opportunity: firms can hire the best candidate regardless of where they live, and people with disabilities or caring responsibilities find it easier to stay in employment.

However, there are genuine costs. Younger employees in particular may struggle to learn their job without watching experienced colleagues at close range, and informal conversations that spark new ideas happen less often on a video call. In addition, the boundary between work and home can blur, so that some people end up working longer hours and feeling isolated.

These problems are serious, but most of them can be reduced. A hybrid model, in which teams meet in person on two or three fixed days a week, preserves mentoring and collaboration while keeping most of the time saved. Clear expectations about working hours can also protect employees from always being available.

Overall, I believe that the advantages of home working outweigh its disadvantages, because the gains in time, flexibility and access are substantial, whereas the main drawbacks can largely be solved through good organisation.

prompt: In many large cities, young people find it increasingly difficult to afford a home. What are the causes of this problem, and what measures could be taken to solve it?
body: In cities such as London, Sydney and Shanghai, many young adults now spend a large proportion of their income on rent and see buying a home as an unrealistic goal. This essay will explain why housing has become so unaffordable and suggest how governments could respond.

The fundamental cause is that the supply of homes has not kept pace with demand. Jobs and universities are concentrated in a few major cities, so people continue to move there, yet strict planning rules and the shortage of land limit how many new homes can be built. A second factor is that property has increasingly become an investment rather than simply a place to live. When interest rates were low, wealthier buyers and investors purchased additional flats, pushing prices further beyond the reach of first-time buyers on ordinary salaries.

Several measures could ease the problem. The most effective long-term solution is to build more, which may require relaxing zoning laws so that apartment blocks can replace low-density housing near transport links. Governments can also build directly, as Singapore has done through its public housing programme, which has allowed the great majority of citizens to own their homes. In the shorter term, higher taxes on second properties and empty homes would discourage speculation and free up existing stock for those who need it.

In conclusion, housing costs have risen mainly because supply is restricted while demand, including investment demand, keeps growing. A combination of more construction, public housing and targeted taxation offers the best chance of giving young people a realistic path to a home of their own.

prompt: Many people now get their news from social media rather than from newspapers or television. Why is this happening? Is it a positive or negative development?
body: Over the past decade, social media platforms have overtaken newspapers and television as the main source of news for many people, especially the young. This essay will examine the reasons for this change and argue that, on balance, it is a negative development.

The shift is easy to explain. Social media is free, constantly updated and always in our pockets, whereas newspapers cost money and television news is broadcast at fixed times. Platforms also personalise what users see, offering stories that match their interests and allowing them to comment and share instantly. For a generation used to on-demand services, this convenience is difficult for traditional media to match.

Some aspects of this change are welcome. Breaking news reaches people within minutes, and ordinary citizens can report events that mainstream outlets might overlook, as happened during several natural disasters when eyewitness videos informed the world before journalists arrived.

Nevertheless, the drawbacks are more significant. Because algorithms reward content that provokes strong reactions, false or exaggerated stories often spread faster than careful reporting. Personalisation can also trap users in so-called filter bubbles, in which they rarely encounter views that challenge their own, which deepens political division. Finally, as advertising money moves to the platforms, many local newspapers have closed, leaving fewer professional journalists to hold powerful people to account.

In conclusion, people turn to social media for news mainly because it is fast, free and tailored to them. Although this brings some benefits, the spread of misinformation and the decline of independent journalism make it, in my view, a largely negative trend.
source: English Lab model answer (written by Claude; not an official IELTS script)

prompt: The table below shows the percentage of household spending on five categories in three countries in 2020. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

figure.caption: Household spending by category, 2020 (% of total). Practice data, invented for this exercise.

body: The table compares how households in three countries divided their spending among five categories in 2020.

Overall, housing was the largest expense in Country A, whereas food dominated budgets in Country C. Households in Country A also devoted a noticeably larger share of their spending to leisure and healthcare than those in the other two countries.

Looking at the essentials first, housing accounted for almost a third of spending in Country A (32%), compared with 24% in Country B and just 18% in Country C. The pattern for food was almost exactly the reverse: it made up 35% of household expenditure in Country C, 22% in Country B and only 14% in Country A.

As for the remaining categories, transport took a broadly similar share everywhere, ranging from 11% in Country C to 17% in Country B. Leisure, however, varied considerably, from 12% in Country A to 9% in Country B and a mere 5% in Country C. Healthcare was the smallest category in all three countries, at between 4% and 8%.

prompt: The graph below shows the number of visitors to three museums in a city between 2010 and 2020. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

figure.caption: Visitors per year (thousands). The line graph's data shown as a table. Practice data, invented for this exercise.

body: The line graph illustrates how many people visited three museums in a city over the decade from 2010 to 2020.

Overall, visitor numbers at the Science Museum and the Art Gallery rose steadily for most of the period, while the History Museum gradually lost popularity. All three, however, saw a dramatic fall in the final year.

In 2010, the History Museum was the most visited, attracting 600,000 people, compared with 420,000 at the Science Museum and 250,000 at the Art Gallery. Over the following eight years, the History Museum declined slowly to 500,000 visitors. In contrast, the Science Museum grew consistently, overtaking the History Museum in 2014 and reaching a peak of 650,000 in 2018.

The Art Gallery showed the fastest growth in the second half of the decade, with visitor numbers almost doubling from 250,000 in 2010 to 470,000 in 2018, so that it was close to the History Museum by the end of that period. In 2020, attendance at every museum roughly halved, falling to between 210,000 and 300,000.

prompt: The diagram below shows how plastic bottles are recycled. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features.

figure.caption: Stages shown in the diagram (practice task).
items: Used bottles are placed in recycling bins
Bottles are collected by truck and taken to a recycling plant
Bottles are sorted by type and colour
Bottles are washed to remove labels and dirt
Bottles are shredded into small flakes
Flakes are melted and formed into pellets
Pellets are used to make new products: bottles, clothing fibres, containers

body: The diagram illustrates the process by which used plastic bottles are recycled and turned into new products.

Overall, the process consists of seven stages, beginning with the collection of used bottles and ending with the manufacture of a range of new goods. Most of the stages take place at a recycling plant.

To begin with, consumers place their empty bottles in recycling bins, from which they are collected by truck and transported to the plant. On arrival, the bottles are sorted according to their type and colour, after which they are washed thoroughly so that labels and any dirt are removed.

Once clean, the bottles are shredded into small flakes. These flakes are then melted down and formed into pellets, which serve as the raw material for manufacturing. Finally, the pellets are used to produce a variety of items, including new bottles, fibres for clothing and other plastic containers, which means that the material can re-enter the cycle.
